headline: The Oldest Migration on the Bay
hook: On a handful of nights each spring, timed to the moon, Delaware Bay hosts what wildlife agencies call the largest horseshoe crab spawning event on Earth — feeding a shorebird that flies here from the bottom of South America and cannot finish the trip without it.
sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Rufa Red Knot species profile and Delaware Bay Rufa Red Knot and Horseshoe Crab FAQ
DNREC, Delaware Bay Horseshoe Crab Spawning Survey
The Conservation Fund, Mispillion Harbor protection history
Smithsonian National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute, horseshoe crab natural history
body: Every May and June, on nights timed to the moon, Delaware Bay hosts one of the largest horseshoe crab spawning events on Earth.
Red knots fly here from the bottom of South America and depend on horseshoe crab eggs to fuel the final leg of their migration to the Arctic.
Conservation of Mispillion Harbor and tighter harvest limits have helped both species begin to recover after a steep decline.

headline: The Galloping Dune
hook: Delaware's tallest sand dune buried a WWII bunker, swallowed a pine forest, and earned its nickname because it used to move. Nearby, part of the park still does.
sources: Delaware State Parks state historical marker, "The Great Dune: Living Sands," Cape Henlopen State Park
Delaware State Parks, Cape Henlopen State Park park description and trail information
body: Cape Henlopen's Great Dune stands about 80 feet above the ocean, built by wind and sand over thousands of years.
Deforestation in the early 1800s set the dune loose, and it moved inland fast enough to earn the nickname 'Galloping Dune.'
The Army added sand to hide a WWII bunker, raising the dune to its current height and stabilizing it; nearby, the Walking Dunes Trail is still actively migrating today.

headline: Where the Marsh Is Going
hook: Nearly half of Delaware's wetlands lie between the tides, quietly filtering water, buffering storms, and raising nearly every fish on your plate. As seas rise, the state's plan isn't to hold the line — it's to let the marsh move.
sources: DNREC, Delaware wetlands acreage data and Marsh Migration in Delaware program materials
DNREC Wildlife Action Plan, tidal wetland nursery habitat and ecosystem service data
Yale Environment 360, "Domino Effect: The Myriad Impacts of Warming on an East Coast Estuary"
Reporting on Bombay Hook and Prime Hook National Wildlife Refuge marsh loss and restoration
body: Delaware's tidal wetlands cover more than 113,000 acres and provide nursery habitat for around 90 percent of the coast's commercially important fish and shellfish.
Bombay Hook National Wildlife Refuge has already lost about 2,000 acres of salt marsh to sea level rise and erosion since the 1970s.
Rather than fighting the water, Delaware's Prime Hook restoration and DNREC's marsh migration program aim to let marshes move inland as seas rise.

headline: The Towers on the Dunes
hook: Every summer thousands of people photograph the concrete towers along the Delaware coast without knowing what they are. They were optical instruments, built to last about ten years.
sources: Delaware Division of Historical and Cultural Affairs, "Fire Control Towers" (history.delaware.gov/preservation/firetowers)
Delaware State Parks and Cape Gazette/WGMD reporting on the 2023 reopening of Tower 3
body: You have seen them: plain cylindrical concrete towers along the Delaware coast, several storeys of grey, with narrow horizontal slits near the top. They are fire control towers, built during the Second World War to aim coastal artillery, and they solved a real problem — a gun crew at ground level cannot judge a warship's distance, course, or speed well enough to hit it.

The solution was triangulation. Observers in two or more towers at precisely surveyed positions took simultaneous bearings on a target, and a plotting room combined those readings into a firing solution for the guns at Fort Miles. The towers were the sensor array of a distributed weapons system — the eyes of guns that could not see for themselves.

By the state's own account the towers were expected to last roughly a decade. The technology they served was approaching obsolescence before the war even ended, as radar replaced optical triangulation. Nobody knocked them down anyway — reinforced concrete built to withstand naval gunfire is difficult and expensive to demolish, so the towers stayed and slowly became landmarks instead of weapons.

Eleven of these towers still stand in Delaware, across Cape Henlopen, Delaware Seashore, and Fenwick Island state parks. Tower 3, at Delaware Seashore State Park, reopened to the public in 2023 with a rebuilt staircase. This publication does not repeat the widely circulated claim that Delaware is the only state with all of its original towers — the state's own published material doesn't make that claim, and we couldn't verify it independently.
heroAlt: Aerial view of the Cape Henlopen coastline where the fire-control towers stand

kicker: How Delaware Became Delaware · Installment 6 of 9
headline: Why Delaware Looks Like That
hook: Delaware's northern boundary is a circular arc, unlike any other state line in the country. It exists because of a property dispute and a survey nobody could execute cleanly.
sources: U.S. National Park Service, "Delaware's 12-Mile Arc" (nps.gov)
Delaware Division of Historical and Cultural Affairs, "Surveying the Landscape of the 'Delaware Wedge'" (history.delaware.gov, 2023)
body: Delaware's northern border curves — a circular arc, unlike any other state line in the country. It began in 1681, when the Duke of York directed that the boundary between his remaining Delaware holdings and William Penn's new Pennsylvania charter be drawn as a circle with a twelve-mile radius centered on New Castle.

Surveying a true twelve-mile arc through colonial forest and swamp was nearly impossible with the instruments available. The first serious attempt, in 1701, wasn't approved by both colonies until 1715–1719. By the mid-1700s the circle's formal center point had been fixed at the cupola of the New Castle Court House, which still stands.

In 1763 Charles Mason and Jeremiah Dixon surveyed the boundary with far better precision, but found the tangent point didn't match earlier surveys — so the North Line cut through the Circle instead of running clear of it. Their fix, the short Arc Line, added a reported thirteen acres to Delaware and left behind a second problem: a leftover triangular parcel called the Wedge.

The Wedge sat in jurisdictional limbo for most of the nineteenth century. A joint commission awarded it to Delaware in 1889; Pennsylvania ratified in 1897; Delaware ratified in 1921; and Congress approved it the same year. Two hundred and forty years after the original 1681 grant, the shape of the state was finally settled — and many of Mason and Dixon's original boundary stones, including ornately carved crownstones, still stand where they were placed.

lede: Delaware's northern boundary is a circular arc — unlike any other state line in the country. It exists because of a property dispute, a survey nobody could execute cleanly, and a case that took two hundred and forty years to finish.

kicker: How Delaware Became Delaware · Installment 7 of 9
headline: Three Counties Become the First State
hook: Delaware declared independence from Britain and Pennsylvania in the same week of 1776 — and eleven years later became the first state to ratify the Constitution, in a rented tavern, unanimously, in five days.
sources: Delaware Public Archives, Ratification Document record
U.S. National Park Service, First State National Historical Park materials
body: In the first week of December 1787, thirty delegates gathered at Battell's Tavern on the Dover Green — the State House wasn't finished yet — to vote on the constitution drafted in Philadelphia that September. They deliberated five days and ratified unanimously on December 7, 1787, making Delaware the first state to ratify the U.S. Constitution.

Getting there took most of a century. Delaware's three counties had been attached to William Penn's Pennsylvania since 1682, mainly because Pennsylvania needed the Delaware River's mouth. The two territories split into separate legislatures in 1704 but kept sharing a governor for 72 more years — an arrangement nobody designed; it accumulated.

Delaware separated from both Britain and Pennsylvania in the same June 1776 session, an event now called the Act of Separation. Caesar Rodney's famous ride to Philadelphia that July, breaking a tied delegation vote on independence, really happened — though the dramatic details usually attached to it go beyond what the documentary record supports.

Delaware's rapid, unanimous ratification in 1787 wasn't primarily patriotic zeal — it was arithmetic. The new Constitution's compromise gave every state equal representation in the Senate, which mattered enormously to one of the smallest states in the union. Being first was a consequence of moving quickly, and moving quickly was a consequence of having already gotten what they needed.

headline: The Six O'Clock Shift at Indian River Inlet
hook: Every morning the surfcasters pack up right as the paddleboarders wade in — a ten-minute handoff between two different Delawares.
body: By 5:40 AM the jetty at Indian River Inlet already has six rods planted in sand spikes, tips bowed slightly toward the current, lines running out into water that's still more black than blue. Nobody's talking much. The regulars know each other by silhouette — the guy in the faded Phillies cap who's been coming out since April, the woman with the two coolers who never seems to leave without at least one keeper.

This is the quiet shift. The bridge traffic hasn't started yet. The bait shop up the road won't open for another twenty minutes. For about an hour and a half, the inlet belongs entirely to people who set an alarm on purpose.

Then, somewhere around 6:50, the light changes from gray to gold, and the handoff starts. A paddleboarder wades in near the calmer water on the bay side. Two more show up with boards under their arms, wetsuits half-zipped, coffee still in hand. By 7:15 there are more boards in the water than rods on the beach, and by 7:30 most of the surfcasters have already reeled in, packed the truck and headed home before the heat sets in.

For about ten minutes, though, both crowds are out there together — lines still in the water, boards drifting past the jetty rocks, everybody polite about staying out of each other's space. Nobody photographs it because it doesn't look like much. But it's one of the only times all day that the inlet holds two completely different versions of a Delaware beach morning at once, and neither one seems to mind sharing.

By 8 AM it's a normal beach day again — families setting up chairs, the bait shop finally open, the bridge humming with cars. The six o'clock shift is over until tomorrow, when it starts all over again, the same quiet handoff, mostly unwatched.

headline: What the Boardwalk Smells Like in July
hook: Grotto pizza, salt water taffy and sunscreen, in that order, from the top of Rehoboth Avenue to the water.
body: Walk onto the Rehoboth boardwalk from Rehoboth Avenue on a July evening and the smell arrives in a specific order, the same one every single night. First it's pizza — the particular sweetness of Grotto's sauce, cut with melted cheese, carrying half a block in either direction. Then, closer to the taffy shops, sugar takes over: warm, slightly burnt, the smell of a candy-pulling machine that's been running all day.

By the time you hit the sand, it's sunscreen and salt air doing all the work, with a faint charcoal drift from someone's beachfront grill a few blocks down. It's a strange, specific combination that doesn't exist anywhere else — not at the mall, not at another beach, not in a candle no matter how hard some company tries.

Locals stop noticing it by June. Visitors notice it every single year, usually saying some version of the same thing: it smells like summer. Not summer in general — this one, specifically, the Rehoboth one, the one that's been more or less the same smell since Dolle's started making taffy on the boardwalk in 1926.
It's worth a slow walk sometime, phone away, just to notice the handoff — pizza to taffy to salt — the whole thing over in about four blocks.

headline: A Field Guide to Bethany's Bandstand Nights
hook: Beach chairs go down by 7, the band starts by 8, and nobody in Bethany seems to be in a hurry to leave once it's over.
body: Bethany's bandstand sits at the center of a boardwalk short enough that you can hear the music from almost any bench on it. On a concert night, the chairs start appearing by 7 — folding, low-slung, the kind that live in a trunk all summer — staked out in a loose semicircle facing the stage.

The bands vary week to week: beach music one night, a cover band leaning hard into 80s hits the next, occasionally something closer to bluegrass. Nobody seems to come for a specific act so much as for the ritual of it — ice cream from the shop across the street, a slow walk down to the water between sets, kids running the same fifty feet of boardwalk back and forth until the second song starts.

What's notable is what doesn't happen. Nobody's rushing off to the next thing. There's no line to get in, no ticket, no VIP section. By 9:30, when the last song wraps up, half the crowd is still sitting there finishing a conversation, in no particular hurry to fold the chairs back up.
If Rehoboth is the Delaware beach for a big night out, Bethany's bandstand is the answer for people who want the whole evening to feel like a long exhale instead.

headline: The Unmarked Trail Behind Gordons Pond
hook: Most people park at Gordons Pond, walk the boardwalk to the beach, and turn around. The trail that keeps going is where the park gets quiet.
body: Gordons Pond's main boardwalk trail does exactly what it's built to do — it gets a steady stream of walkers from the parking lot straight out to the beach, flat and easy, done in about twenty-five minutes round trip. Most visitors do exactly that and call it a day.

But where the boardwalk crosses back inland, a narrower dirt path splits off through the maritime forest instead of returning to the lot directly. It's marked, technically, with small blazes easy to miss if you're not looking down — which is probably why so few people take it.

The path winds through loblolly pine and holly thickets, opens briefly onto marsh views facing the bay, and stays noticeably cooler than the open dune trail in July. It adds maybe forty minutes to the walk, and for most of it, the loudest sound is wind moving through pine needles instead of the ocean.

It loops back to the main lot eventually, no navigation required, no risk of getting lost. But for a park that gets genuinely crowded on summer weekends, it's the closest thing to solitude Cape Henlopen offers — and it's sitting in plain sight the whole time, mostly unbothered.

headline: Low Tide at Assateague Is a Different Island
hook: When the water pulls back, the horses come down off the dunes to graze flats that don't exist three hours later.
body: At high tide, Assateague reads the way most people picture it — dunes, beach grass, horses grazing somewhere up in the marsh, distant enough to need binoculars. At low tide, the whole island rearranges itself.

Wide sand and mud flats emerge along the bay side, and the horses come down off higher ground to graze on the exposed marsh grass, sometimes close enough to a quiet trail that a long lens isn't strictly necessary. Shorebirds move in behind them, working the same flats for whatever the tide left behind.

It lasts a few hours, tide-dependent, and then it's gone — water creeps back in, the horses drift back to higher ground, and the island returns to its regular, more distant version of itself. Checking the tide chart before a visit is worth the extra two minutes; showing up at the wrong tide means missing the whole show entirely.
It's a reminder that Assateague was never really built for a schedule. The island runs on its own clock, and the best visits are the ones that show up to match it instead of the other way around.

headline: The Last Seventeen Hundred
hook: Delaware refused to abolish slavery in February 1865 — for fewer than 1,800 people, in a state where nine in ten Black Delawareans were already free. The Emancipation Proclamation never applied here, and the legislature did not ratify the Thirteenth Amendment until 1901.
lede: Delaware refused to abolish slavery in February 1865 — for fewer than 1,800 people, in a state where nine in ten Black Delawareans were already free.
heroAlt: Delaware marsh at first light
heroImageAlt: Illustration of a Delaware marsh at dawn
author: first-state-history
sources: U.S. Census of 1860, Delaware enslaved and free Black population counts
University of Delaware, Black History in Delaware: the antebellum free African American community
National Archives, Milestone Documents: 13th Amendment
WHYY reporting on emancipation and Delaware's enslaved population
Contemporary accounts of the Delaware General Assembly resolution of February 8, 1865
body: Delaware's legislature declared its 'unqualified disapproval' of the Thirteenth Amendment on February 8, 1865, and refused to ratify it.
By the 1860 census Delaware held 1,798 people in slavery while roughly 92 percent of Black Delawareans were already free — the highest proportion in any slave state.
The Emancipation Proclamation did not apply to Delaware, which had not seceded. Slavery ended there only when the amendment was ratified nationally in December 1865. Delaware ratified it in 1901.
seoTitle: The Last Seventeen Hundred: Delaware and the Thirteenth Amendment
seoDescription: Delaware rejected the Thirteenth Amendment in February 1865 and did not ratify it until 1901. Why a state that had already freed nine in ten Black Delawareans held on to slavery to the last legal day.

headline: In His Boots and Spurs
hook: The most famous sentence about Caesar Rodney's ride was written thirty-seven years later, by a man correcting somebody else's version of events. What the record actually supports — and why Delaware needed the story.
lede: The most famous sentence about Caesar Rodney's ride was written thirty-seven years later, by a man correcting somebody else's version of events.
heroAlt: Delaware dunes at sunrise
heroImageAlt: Illustration of Delaware dunes at sunrise
author: first-state-history
sources: Thomas McKean to Caesar A. Rodney, 22 September 1813, Papers of Thomas Jefferson, Founders Online, U.S. National Archives
National Park Service, Caesar Rodney Statue and Rodney's ride materials
U.S. Mint, 1999 Delaware state quarter
Standard reference accounts of the ride giving the distance as 70 miles
body: The 'boots and spurs' detail comes from Thomas McKean's letter of 22 September 1813, written 37 years after the event to correct a relative's mistaken account.
Authorities disagree on the distance: the National Park Service says nearly 80 miles, standard accounts say 70, and no contemporaneous figure is known.
The modern image of the ride derives largely from James Edward Kelly's 1923 statue, the musical 1776, and the 1999 Delaware quarter.
seoTitle: In His Boots and Spurs: Caesar Rodney's Ride, Myth and Record
seoDescription: What the documentary record actually supports about Caesar Rodney's July 1776 ride — the 1813 letter behind the famous detail, the ten-mile disagreement over distance, and why Delaware needed the story.

headline: The Colony That Failed and Stayed
hook: New Sweden lasted seventeen years and surrendered without a shot. Almost everybody who lived there stayed for good — and by staying, made the lower Delaware a different place from the province upriver.
lede: New Sweden lasted seventeen years and surrendered without a shot. Almost everybody who lived there stayed for good.
heroAlt: Delaware Bay at first light
heroImageAlt: Illustration of Delaware Bay at first light
author: first-state-history
sources: Delaware Public Archives, historical markers: Landing of the Swedes; Fort Christina
Kalmar Nyckel Foundation, history of the original Kalmar Nyckel and the 1638 expedition
Swedish Colonial Society, Chronology of Colonial Swedes on the Delaware, 1638-1713
National Park Service, First State National Historical Park materials on Fort Christina
body: Two ships under Peter Minuit reached the Christina River in March 1638 and built Fort Christina, the first permanent European settlement in the Delaware Valley.
New Sweden surrendered to Peter Stuyvesant in 1655 without a fight, but most Swedish and Finnish settlers stayed and kept a measure of self-government under Dutch and then English rule.
That persistence is why the Three Lower Counties were culturally distinct from Quaker Pennsylvania when the two later separated.
seoTitle: New Sweden: The Colony That Failed and Stayed
seoDescription: New Sweden lasted seventeen years on the Delaware River and surrendered without a shot in 1655. Why the settlers stayed, what the 1638 land transaction did and did not settle, and how a failed colony shaped the Three Lower Counties.

headline: The Ladder off Cape Henlopen
hook: Most days and nights of the year, someone climbs a rope ladder up the side of a moving ship east of Cape Henlopen. It is how every large vessel enters Delaware Bay, and it has been happening here since 1650.
lede: Most days and nights of the year, someone climbs a rope ladder up the side of a moving ship east of Cape Henlopen.
heroAlt: Fenwick Island Lighthouse, one of Delaware's coastal navigation landmarks
heroImageAlt: The Fenwick Island Lighthouse tower against a clear sky
author: coast-nature
sources: The Pilots' Association for the Bay and River Delaware
Reference accounts of the association's founding at Lewes, 28 November 1896
Act of the first United States Congress, 1789, leaving pilotage regulation to the states
Delaware pilotage legislation of 1881 establishing a board of commissioners
body: Every large vessel entering Delaware Bay takes aboard a state-licensed pilot, who boards by climbing a ladder onto a moving ship east of Cape Henlopen.
The Pilots' Association for the Bay and River Delaware organised at Lewes on 28 November 1896, ending a competitive era in which pilot schooners raced seaward for work.
Pilotage on the Delaware is traditionally dated to 1650 — when the colony on this river was New Sweden and Delaware did not yet exist.
seoTitle: The Ladder off Cape Henlopen: The Delaware Bay Pilots
seoDescription: How every large ship enters Delaware Bay: the state-licensed pilots who board from a launch east of Cape Henlopen, the association founded at Lewes in 1896, and a job older than the state itself.

headline: The Attic in Dover
hook: Every astronomer alive sorts stars using a system worked out by a shipbuilder's daughter from Dover. Annie Jump Cannon classified roughly 350,000 stars by eye — more than any human being who has ever lived.
lede: Every astronomer alive sorts stars using a system worked out by a shipbuilder's daughter from Dover.
heroAlt: A Delaware pier at night
heroImageAlt: Illustration of a Delaware pier under a night sky
author: delaware-life
sources: Harvard College Observatory and Wolbach Library materials on Annie Jump Cannon and the Harvard Computers
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Annie Jump Cannon
National Women's History Museum biography
Reference accounts of the Henry Draper Catalogue and the 1922 IAU adoption of the Harvard spectral classification
body: Annie Jump Cannon, born in Dover in 1863 to a shipbuilder and state senator, learned the constellations from her mother in the family attic.

Hired at Harvard College Observatory in 1896, she reconciled two competing classification schemes into the O B A F G K M sequence, ordered by Balmer absorption line strength — which turned out to order stars by temperature.
She classified roughly 350,000 stars by eye, at times three a minute, and the IAU adopted her system in 1922. It has not been replaced.
seoTitle: The Attic in Dover: Annie Jump Cannon, Delaware's Astronomer
seoDescription: Annie Jump Cannon of Dover, Delaware classified roughly 350,000 stars by eye and created the O B A F G K M system every astronomer still uses. How a shipbuilder's daughter reorganised the sky.

headline: The Standing Dead
hook: Bare trunks standing in open marsh along Delaware Bay look like an ending. They are the opposite: they mark the line where the marsh is climbing inland — which is the only escape route it has.
lede: Bare trunks standing in open marsh along Delaware Bay look like an ending. They are the leading edge of something moving.
heroAlt: Standing dead trees in a Delaware marsh at dusk
heroImageAlt: Bare trunks of a ghost forest standing in marsh at dusk
author: coast-nature
sources: Delaware DNREC, Wetland Monitoring and Assessment Program, on saltwater intrusion and marsh migration
Peer-reviewed lidar and imagery analysis of coastal forest loss around Delaware Bay
Scientific literature on ghost forest formation along the US Atlantic coast
body: Repeated saltwater flooding changes coastal forest soil chemistry until sensitive trees die, leaving standing dead trunks along the marsh edge.
DNREC describes marsh migration upslope into forest as the last hope for much of Delaware's tidal marsh as sea level rises.
Where a marsh is backed by a bulkhead, road or hard shoreline it cannot migrate, and is squeezed against the barrier instead.
seoTitle: The Standing Dead: Delaware Bay's Ghost Forests
seoDescription: Why bare trees stand in the marsh along Delaware Bay, how saltwater intrusion kills a coastal forest, and why the ghost forest is the marsh escaping inland rather than the marsh dying.

headline: Read the Apron
hook: The most useful thing to know about crabbing in Delaware is how to turn a crab over. The shape on its belly tells you what you are holding, whether you can keep it, and whether you should.
lede: The most useful thing to know about crabbing in Delaware is how to turn a crab over.
heroAlt: A basket of Delaware blue crabs
heroImageAlt: Blue crabs in a basket
author: field-notes
sources: Delaware DNREC recreational fishing and shellfishing regulations for blue crabs
DNREC Delaware Fish Facts, blue crab
body: A blue crab's apron identifies it: narrow and tapered is a male, triangular is an immature female, broad and rounded is a mature female.
Delaware requires a recreational fishing licence for crabbing, sets a five-inch hard-shell minimum, allows mature females at any size, and prohibits taking egg-bearing sponge crabs.
Regulations change; DNREC publishes the current rules and should be checked before a trip.
seoTitle: Read the Apron: A Delaware Blue Crab Field Guide
seoDescription: How to tell a jimmy from a sook from a sponge crab, what Delaware's crabbing rules actually require, and why throwing back egg-bearing females is the whole game.

headline: Three Hundred Dollars
hook: In 1907 a doctor outside Wilmington needed $300 to keep a tuberculosis sanatorium open through the winter. His cousin raised ten times that by selling penny stamps that carried no mail — and accidentally founded a national institution.
lede: In the autumn of 1907 a doctor outside Wilmington needed three hundred dollars, and wrote to his cousin about it.

sources: Smithsonian National Postal Museum, Emily Bissell

University of Virginia Historical Collections, Christmas Seals and the anti-tuberculosis movement
The Lancet Respiratory Medicine, profile of Emily Perkins Bissell
body: Emily Perkins Bissell of Wilmington was asked in 1907 to raise $300 to keep the Brandywine Sanatorium open through the winter.
Borrowing an idea from a Jacob Riis article about a Danish scheme, she designed and sold penny Christmas Seals through the Delaware Red Cross, raising roughly $3,000.
The campaign went national in 1908 and ran for the better part of a century; the sanatorium was renamed the Emily P. Bissell Hospital in 1957.
seoTitle: Three Hundred Dollars: Emily Bissell and the First Christmas Seals
seoDescription: How Emily Bissell of Wilmington raised ten times her target in 1907 by selling penny stamps that carried no mail, saved the Brandywine Sanatorium, and started a national fundraising institution.

headline: The Patience of Herons
hook: A great blue heron stands four feet tall, spans six feet, and weighs about as much as a housecat. Almost everything it does is waiting — and the strike, when it comes, is one of the fastest things a large animal does.
lede: A great blue heron hunting looks, for long stretches, like a bird that has forgotten what it was doing.
heroAlt: A great blue heron landing on Delaware marsh water
heroImageAlt: A great blue heron landing with wings spread over shallow water
author: coast-nature
sources: Audubon field guide, great blue heron
Delaware DNREC, Outdoor Delaware, on Delaware's heron species
Standard reference accounts of great blue heron size and weight
body: The great blue heron is North America's largest heron, about four feet tall with a six-foot wingspan, weighing only five or six pounds.
It hunts by standing still or moving very slowly, then striking with a rapid thrust of the bill; the stillness is the technique, not rest.
The widely repeated claim that Delaware hosts the largest heron gathering north of Florida could not be verified and is not asserted here.
seoTitle: The Patience of Herons: Delaware's Great Blue Herons
seoDescription: How a great blue heron actually hunts, why a four-foot bird weighs six pounds, where to find them in Delaware, and the Pea Patch Island claim this publication will not repeat unverified.

headline: The Refuge Loop
hook: Delaware's two national wildlife refuges are best watched from inside a car, on a falling tide, with the engine off. Everything else about Bombay Hook and Prime Hook follows from getting that right.
lede: Delaware has two national wildlife refuges on its bay shore, and the useful thing to understand about both is that you watch them from your car.
heroAlt: A great blue heron in low flight over Delaware marsh
heroImageAlt: A great blue heron flying low over marsh water with its reflection beneath
author: field-notes
sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Bombay Hook National Wildlife Refuge
U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Prime Hook National Wildlife Refuge
Audubon guidance on wading bird observation
body: Bombay Hook and Prime Hook are best birded from a stopped vehicle; the car functions as a hide.
A falling tide concentrates prey and pulls wading birds in to feed, making it the most productive time to visit.
Refuge hours, access and closures are set by the refuges and should be checked before travelling.
seoTitle: The Refuge Loop: Birding Bombay Hook and Prime Hook
seoDescription: How to actually watch Delaware's national wildlife refuges: why the car is the hide, why a falling tide beats a clock, what to bring, and how to look at a marsh without missing what is standing in it.

headline: What the Dunes Were For
hook: The parking lot at Cape Henlopen sits on top of a gun battery. Delaware's most-visited state park is laid over a coastal fortress built to close the mouth of Delaware Bay — and the only enemy warship that ever arrived came in flying a surrender signal.
lede: The parking lot at Cape Henlopen sits on top of a gun battery. Not near one. On one.
heroAlt: The Delaware coast from the air, where the Atlantic meets Delaware Bay
heroImageAlt: Aerial view of the Delaware coastline at sunset
author: first-state-history
sources: Fort Miles Museum / Fort Miles Historical Association, history of Fort Miles
Delaware State Parks, Fort Miles Museum and Historical Area at Cape Henlopen State Park
U.S. Naval History and Heritage Command, surrender of German submarine U-858, 14 May 1945
Reference accounts of Battery 519 construction and the 1964 establishment of Cape Henlopen State Park
body: Fort Miles was built on Cape Henlopen between 1941 and 1944 to close the entrance to Delaware Bay and protect the Delaware River industrial corridor, including the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard.
At its peak it held roughly 2,500 soldiers and civilian personnel and around a dozen batteries, from 155mm mobile guns up to the 16-inch guns of Battery Smith.
The guns never fired on an enemy ship. The only enemy warship to arrive was U-858, which surrendered at Lewes on 14 May 1945 — the first enemy warship to surrender in US waters since the War of 1812.
seoTitle: What the Dunes Were For: Fort Miles and Delaware's WWII Coast
seoDescription: Cape Henlopen State Park is built over Fort Miles, the fortress that closed the mouth of Delaware Bay in the Second World War. Why the bay mattered, what the guns were for, and the U-boat that surrendered at Lewes in 1945.
